notes.text:
# Partition study notebook

## Prior expectations

**H1 [tentative] — material pairing.** Target partition may depend on the solvent-S/extractant-X pair; anonymous indices carry no ordering or identity. A broad pair screen should reveal whether pair effects exceed HPLC uncertainty.

**H2 [tentative] — phase amount.** At fixed pairing and equilibration, increasing organic share should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory in the organic phase, even if the concentration-based distribution coefficient is unchanged.

**H3 [tentative] — mixing.** More vigorous/longer mixing should approach an equilibrium plateau; inadequate mixing may lower observed transfer. A repeat at a common condition is needed to gauge process plus instrument scatter.

**Predictions before data:** two-phase HPLC before separation should show product fractions in both phases and a phase ratio consistent with actual combined volumes (including initial liquid and additions). Retaining organic after settling should preserve the organic-associated target fraction; retaining aqueous should instead preserve the aqueous-associated fraction. These are qualitative expectations and will be revised if contradicted.

## Planned scope
Twelve independent batches from the same initial mixture. Use one pre-separation HPLC per batch (all 12 nonfinal uses), vary pairings, phase amounts, and mixing, include a replicate, then deliberately retain organic or aqueous and obtain the required post-termination final assay. No unmeasured quantity will be treated as zero.

# Partition study notebook

## Prior expectations

**H1 [supported within screened pairs; interaction unresolved] — material pairing.** At nominal volumes (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous addition, 0.02 L extractant) and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, pairing changes the organic inventory fraction substantially. With S0, X0/X1/X2/X3 gave pre-separation HPLC organic fractions about 0.297, 0.497, 0.380, 0.558 (events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037; each stated SD 0.015). With X0, S0/S1/S2/S3 gave about 0.297, 0.485, 0.401, 0.521 (events -0007, -0047, -0057, -0067). Differences are numerical and mostly much larger than individual instrument SD, but each nonbaseline pair currently lacks process replication. Solvent and extractant labels are independent anonymous categories; no ordinal interpretation is made. A diagonal pair will probe whether effects are simply additive; full interaction mapping is unavailable with this budget.

**H2 [tentative] — phase amount.** Increasing extractant/organic share is still predicted to increase organic inventory fraction. Current nominal observed phase ratios vary 0.169–0.219 despite identical additions, more than expected from stated HPLC SD alone, suggesting material-dependent phase volumes and/or process variability; therefore actual measured phase ratio must be used rather than addition ratio.

**H3 [tentative] — mixing.** More vigorous/longer mixing should approach a plateau; a deliberately weak mix and a nominal repeat are reserved to test this.

**H4 [supported qualitatively] — retention.** After separation, organic-retained final assays show phase ratio near 1 and preserve organic target inventory close to the pre-separation HPLC estimate (events runner-operation-0010, -0020, -0040, -0050, -0070). Aqueous-retained assays show phase ratio 0 and preserve aqueous rather than organic inventory (events -0030 and -0060). Small nonretained-phase estimates are compatible with assay noise/sampling, not assumed physical zeros.

## Remaining discriminating tests (predictions recorded before execution)
1. One diagonal pair at nominal conditions to extend material coverage.
2. At S0/X1, compare low-extractant/high-aqueous and high-extractant/low-aqueous conditions; predict measured phase ratio and organic inventory fraction rise together.
3. At S0/X1 nominal volumes, weak 10 s/100 rpm mixing should give no higher organic transfer than 300 s/600 rpm if approach-to-equilibrium is monotone; a nominal repeat will assess repeatability. One nominal batch will retain aqueous to verify the retention decision under the same pair.

## Limits tracked
Product fractions refer to fixed initial inventory, not concentrations. HPLC is pre-separation/two-phase; final assay is post-removal. Solvent and initial liquid contribute to actual volume, so addition volumes alone do not define phase ratio.

# Partition study notebook

## Final source-stage interpretation

**H1 [supported in screened scope; interactions incompletely mapped] — material pairing matters.** At nominal additions and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, pre-separation organic inventory fractions differed across materials. S0 with X0/X1/X2/X3 gave about 0.297/0.497/0.380/0.558 (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037); X0 with S0/S1/S2/S3 gave about 0.297/0.485/0.401/0.521 (-0007, -0047, -0057, -0067). Individual HPLC SD was 0.015, so many contrasts are substantially larger than analytical noise, though unreplicated process variation remains. S3/X3 gave 0.466 (-0077), showing that good individual row/column levels do not simply guarantee their combination is highest; additive versus interaction mechanisms remain unresolved. Anonymous categories are not ordered and no chemical identity is inferred.

**H2 [supported directionally, not as a universal constant-D law] — actual phase share predicts inventory partition.** For S0/X1, increasing extractant addition from 0.02 to 0.06 L (while reducing other additions to keep total fill) increased measured organic phase ratio from the nominal-replicate range 0.195–0.219 to 0.609 and organic inventory fraction from about 0.482–0.500 to 0.818 (runner-operation-0017, -0117, -0097). The high-aqueous/low-solvent condition had phase ratio 0.194 and organic fraction 0.505 (-0087), emphasizing that aqueous addition alone is not total aqueous volume and actual measured phase ratio is the appropriate volume variable.

A concentration-ratio diagnostic derived from HPLC inventories, D=(Porg/Paq)(1-r)/r, was approximately 3.30 and 4.12 for the two nominal well-mixed S0/X1 runs, 4.26 for high-aqueous/low-solvent, 2.89 for high-extractant, and 2.55 for weak mixing. Thus a useful first approximation is q_org = D r/(1-r+D r), with pair- and mixing-specific D, but evidence opposes treating D as precisely invariant across volume/composition. No propagated error model or concentration assay was available, so these are diagnostics, not fitted physical constants.

**H3 [supported for tested contrast] — mixing controls approach to partition.** At S0/X1 nominal volumes, weak 10 s/100 rpm mixing yielded organic inventory 0.405 and derived D about 2.55 (-0107), lower than 0.497 and 0.512 (D about 3.30 and 4.12) in the two 300 s/600 rpm runs (-0017, -0117). The two well-mixed organic fractions differ by only ~0.015, comparable to one stated HPLC SD and below the quadrature of two SDs; this provides limited repeatability evidence. Only two mixing regimes were tested, so kinetics, rpm-duration tradeoff, and true equilibrium plateau remain unresolved.

**H4 [supported] — retention determines what remains.** Organic-retained final assays had phase ratio near 1 and organic inventory close to the pre-separation organic estimate (e.g. -0020, -0040, -0050, -0070, -0080, -0090, -0100, -0110). Aqueous-retained assays had phase ratio 0 and preserved aqueous inventory while organic signal was near zero but not inferred to be zero (-0030, -0060, -0120). For S0/X1 nominal repeat, pre-separation Paq=0.513/Porg=0.512 (-0117), while aqueous retention gave final Paq=0.524/Porg=0.0039 (-0120), directly validating the phase-retention interpretation within assay noise and sampling differences.

## Predictive scope and unresolved alternatives

For an untested condition within these ranges, predict the organic inventory using the measured phase ratio plus a pair-specific effective D estimated only from comparable, adequately mixed runs; retain organic when the goal is the organic-associated portion and aqueous when the aqueous-associated portion is sought. Expect higher organic share to raise organic inventory, but widen uncertainty for changed solvent/extractant pairing, extreme composition, or weak mixing. Material effects could represent equilibrium affinity, phase-volume changes, or unmeasured emulsion/settling behavior. Purity/impurity also changed at high extractant (HPLC impurity 0.098 at -0097), so inventory gains are not evidence of a single clean equilibrium mechanism. Initial target closure Porg+Paq varied around unity under HPLC noise/sampling and was never forced to one.

## Evidence limits

Twelve independent batches, one pre-separation HPLC and one final assay each; 12/12 completed and none discarded. Most pair conditions were single runs; only S0/X1 nominal well-mixed had a repeat. Phase ratio is organic volume divided by total two-phase volume and was observed, not reconstructed from additions. Final assays occurred after phase removal and cannot be substituted for missing two-phase measurements.

payload.report:
Account of partition behavior

Observations: All 12 batches began with 0.020 mol reagent and were analyzed by HPLC after mixing and 300 s settling, before phase removal; a final assay followed retention of one phase. At the nominal 0.040 L solvent/0.040 L aqueous/0.020 L extractant condition and 300 s, 600 rpm mixing, material choice strongly affected the measured target inventory. Holding S0 fixed, X0, X1, X2 and X3 gave organic-product fractions of 0.297, 0.497, 0.380 and 0.558 in batches 1–4 (HPLC events 0007, 0017, 0027 and 0037). Holding X0 fixed, S0, S1, S2 and S3 gave 0.297, 0.485, 0.401 and 0.521 in batches 1, 5, 6 and 7 (events 0007, 0047, 0057 and 0067). The stated HPLC SD for each product fraction was 0.015, so most of these contrasts exceed analytical noise, although most conditions were not process-replicated. The S3/X3 diagonal condition produced 0.466 in batch 8 (event 0077), showing that favorable levels from separate row/column comparisons do not simply combine into the highest partition.

Phase amount had a large effect for S0/X1. Nominal well-mixed batches 2 and 12 had measured organic phase ratios of 0.219 and 0.195 and organic fractions of 0.497 and 0.512 (events 0017 and 0117). Raising extractant from 0.020 to 0.060 L while reducing the other additions raised the measured phase ratio to 0.609 and the organic fraction to 0.827 in batch 10 (event 0097). Conversely, the high-aqueous/low-solvent batch 9 still had a phase ratio of 0.194 and organic fraction of 0.496 (event 0087). Thus supplied addition volumes alone did not specify the actual phase ratio; the observed phase ratio was the more useful predictor.

Mixing also mattered. At nominal S0/X1 volumes, deliberately weak mixing for 10 s at 100 rpm gave organic product 0.405 in batch 11 (event 0107), compared with 0.497 and 0.512 after 300 s at 600 rpm in batches 2 and 12. The two adequately mixed replicates differed by only about 0.015, comparable to one HPLC SD. This supports incomplete transfer under the weak condition, but only two mixing regimes were tested.

Phase-retention behavior was internally consistent. Organic-retained final assays generally reported phase ratios near 1 and retained organic target amounts close to their pre-separation estimates—for example batches 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 (final events 0020, 0040, 0050, 0070, 0080, 0090, 0100 and 0110). Aqueous-retained batches 3, 6 and 12 reported phase ratio 0 and preserved aqueous rather than organic target. The clearest matched example is batch 12: pre-separation HPLC gave aqueous 0.513 and organic 0.512; after retaining aqueous, the final assay gave aqueous 0.524 and organic 0.0039 (events 0117 and 0120). Small signals in the removed phase were treated as noise or residual carryover, not exact physical zeros.

Inference: A useful representation is that the organic inventory fraction increases with actual organic phase share, modulated strongly by a material-pair-specific effective affinity and by progress toward equilibration. As a diagnostic—not an imposed law—I calculated an effective concentration ratio from the two inventory fractions and measured phase ratio. For S0/X1 it was approximately 3.30 and 4.12 in the two nominal well-mixed runs, 4.26 in the high-aqueous/low-solvent run, 2.89 in the high-extractant run and 2.55 under weak mixing. This explains why increasing organic phase share strongly increased organic inventory while also showing that a single precisely invariant coefficient is not justified. For prediction within the studied range, measured phase ratio, pair identity and adequate mixing should all be retained as explanatory variables.

Contribution of supplied information: The material packet explicitly provided only opaque S0–S3 and X0–X3 labels, warned that equal indices imply no shared identity or property, and supplied no property dossier. Consequently, no chemical polarity or identity assumptions entered the interpretation; all pair rankings are empirical. Instrument contracts supplied the observable definitions and uncertainty scales: HPLC product-fraction SD 0.015 and phase-ratio SD 0.018, with final-assay product SD 0.010 and phase-ratio SD 0.012. Those scales were used to distinguish large material/mixing contrasts from small replicate differences. The experiments contributed the pair screen, one diagonal combination, controlled phase-amount contrasts, a weak-mixing contrast, a nominal replicate and both retention decisions.

Competing explanations and uncertain scope: The apparent material effects could reflect equilibrium affinity, material-dependent phase volumes, interfacial transport, emulsification or settling behavior rather than one molecular partition mechanism. Solvent amount and extractant amount were necessarily changed together in the volume contrasts, so composition and volume effects are partly confounded. The high-extractant batch also had elevated HPLC impurity signal (0.098), so its target gain does not establish a clean two-component equilibrium. The weak-mixing result supports kinetic limitation but does not determine whether duration, rpm, interfacial area or emulsion resolution was controlling, nor prove that 300 s reached equilibrium. Most pairings had one batch, only a subset of the 16 possible pairs was tested, and no additional mixing times or repeated extreme-volume conditions were measured. Product fractions occasionally failed exact unit closure within measurement/process variability, so they were not renormalized or treated as exact mass balances. The account should therefore be applied only to these anonymous materials, approximate fill range and tested mixing/settling protocol, with wider uncertainty for untested pairs or more extreme compositions.

payload.rationale: Predictions use the measured campaign pattern that organic inventory rises with extractant-derived phase share, modified by material pairing and incomplete mixing. S0/X3 consistently favored organic transfer over S0/X0, so Q06 exceeds Q05; Q01's small organic share leaves most target aqueous. Longer or faster mixing is treated as near the observed well-mixed plateau. Intervals exclude instrument noise but include process uncertainty, volume extrapolation, and especially the unmeasured S2/X3 interaction.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific mechanistic prior was supplied: the material packet gave only opaque labels and explicitly warned against inferring properties from their indices. The least-tested self-developed rule is therefore the transferability of a pair-specific effective distribution tendency across phase amounts and mixing conditions. In particular, S2/X3 was never tested. Batch 8 (S3/X3) already showed that combining favorable single-material effects need not be additive, so the extrapolation used for S2/X3 is especially vulnerable. A second questionable assumption is that noiseless aqueous and organic target fractions sum exactly to one; the campaign showed approximate closure, but batch 10’s elevated impurity signal leaves genuine target loss as an alternative.

2. I would run one S2/X3 batch at the Q08/Q12 amounts: 0.020 L S2, 0.015 L aqueous phase and 0.019 L X3, using 600 s at 1200 rpm followed by 300 s settling. Before removing either phase, I would measure HPLC phase ratio, target in both phases, impurity signal and recovery. This directly tests the largest unsupported extrapolation while using strong mixing to reduce kinetic ambiguity. An organic fraction near the sealed prediction of 0.74, with reasonable closure and low impurity, would support transferring the S2 and X3 main effects. A result nearer the S2/X0 behavior—roughly 0.55–0.60 at this phase share—or below it would favor a strong adverse pair interaction. A low organic fraction accompanied by poor recovery or high impurity would instead suggest target loss or composition-dependent chemistry, while a low value with good closure would more specifically indicate equilibrium or phase-compatibility interaction.

3. Underused evidence included purity, recovery and impurity channels, especially batch 10’s HPLC impurity signal of 0.098, and the observed variation in phase ratio among nominally identical fills. The terminal assays were used mainly to validate phase retention; their recovery and impurity patterns could have been analyzed more deeply for target loss or carryover. Raw characterization artifacts were also not inspected beyond processed estimates.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q08, Q11 and Q12 because all use the unmeasured S2/X3 pair; their wide intervals acknowledge but cannot calibrate that interaction uncertainty. Q03 and Q04 extrapolate S0/X3 to substantially different phase shares, while Q09 and Q10 interpolate mixing behavior from only two previously tested regimes. There is a real tension between report and predictions: the report said actual measured phase ratio was preferable to addition ratios, but the predictions necessarily reconstructed phase share from supplied volumes. The report also rejected a precisely invariant distribution coefficient, whereas the point predictions used simplified effective coefficients. Finally, the predictions forced aqueous and organic fractions to be complementary, although the report noted imperfect experimental closure and possible impurity formation. These are modeling simplifications, not changes to the sealed outputs, and they make the prediction points appear more definite than the evidence warrants.
